chapters.title: The hidden muscle under your lungs

lines.cap: You breathe about **22,000** times a day, without even thinking about it.
Yet your lungs can't pull in a single breath by themselves. So what makes the air rush in? And why would your lungs be useless on the Moon?
This is **breathing and gas exchange**: how your lungs take in the **oxygen** your cells need, and get rid of the waste gas **carbon dioxide**.
Let's follow a breath down your airways, find out what really moves the air, and watch oxygen cross into your blood.
First, three words that often get muddled: **breathing**, **gas exchange** and **respiration**. Getting them right is an easy way to gain marks.
**Breathing**, also called **ventilation**, is the physical **movement of air** in and out of your lungs.
It's done by muscles: your **diaphragm**, and the muscles between your ribs. It just moves air. It isn't a chemical reaction.
**Gas exchange** is the **swapping of gases** between the air in your lungs and your blood.
**Oxygen** moves from the air into your blood, and **carbon dioxide** moves from your blood into the air. It happens by **diffusion**.
**Respiration** is a **chemical reaction** inside your cells. It uses oxygen to release energy from glucose.
Its word equation: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**, and energy is released.
So here's the order. You **breathe** to bring fresh air into your lungs, and **gas exchange** loads its oxygen into your blood.
Then your blood carries the oxygen to your cells, where **respiration** uses it.
So breathing is **not** respiration. Hold your breath, and your breathing stops, but your cells keep on respiring.

chapters.title: The parts of the respiratory system

lines.cap: Air reaches deep into your chest through a set of branching tubes, like an **upside-down tree**.
It comes in through your **nose** or mouth. The nose is best: it **warms**, **moistens** and **filters** the air.
Then it goes down the **trachea**, or windpipe, at the front of your neck.
**C-shaped rings of cartilage** hold the trachea open, so it can't collapse when you breathe in.
Its lining has two kinds of cell. **Goblet cells** make sticky **mucus**, which traps dust and germs.
**Ciliated cells** have tiny hairs called **cilia**, which **sweep** the mucus and dirt up to your throat, to be swallowed.
It's a **mucus escalator**, keeping your lungs clean.
The trachea splits into two **bronchi**, one to each lung. Just one is a **bronchus**.
Each bronchus branches again and again, into smaller and smaller tubes called **bronchioles**.
At the very ends are tiny air sacs called **alveoli**, where gas exchange happens. Just one is an **alveolus**.
You have around **300 to 500 million** of them.
To remember the order: **T**all **B**rontosaurs **B**reathe **A**ir. Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
Around them are two spongy **lungs**, a cage of **ribs** with **intercostal muscles** between them, and the **diaphragm**, a dome of muscle below.
Each lung is wrapped in slippery **pleural membranes**, with fluid between, so the lungs slide smoothly and stay stuck to the chest wall.

chapters.title: How you breathe in and out

lines.cap: Your lungs can't inflate themselves: they have no muscles that pull air in.
Instead, muscles change the **volume** of your chest, and air follows a simple rule: gas moves from **high pressure** to **low pressure**.
Breathing in. Your **diaphragm contracts** and **flattens**, moving down.
At the same time, your **intercostal muscles contract**, pulling your ribcage **up and out**.
Your chest gets bigger, so its **volume increases**.
The air inside spreads out, so its **pressure falls**, below the pressure of the air outside.
So air **rushes in** to fill your lungs. You don't really pull it in: the air outside **pushes** it in.
Breathing out is the reverse. The diaphragm and intercostals **relax**, so the diaphragm domes back up, and the ribs drop **down and in**.
The chest **volume decreases**, so the **pressure rises** above the air outside, and air is **pushed out**.
So remember the chain: **volume up, pressure down, air in**. **Volume down, pressure up, air out**.
Quiet breathing out is mostly **passive**: your stretched lungs just spring back.
For breathing **IN**, think of the letter **I**: the diaphragm d**i**ps, the ribs r**i**se, the volume r**i**ses, the pressure d**i**ps.
Try it at home: a bottle with its bottom cut off, a balloon 'lung' inside, and a stretched balloon 'diaphragm' across the bottom.
Pull the diaphragm down, and the lung inflates. Push it up, and it deflates.
And on the Moon? There's no air outside to push in, so your lungs would be useless.
Each alveolus is wrapped in a dense net of **capillaries**, the smallest blood vessels.
Here the gases swap places, entirely by **diffusion**: a substance spreading from a **high concentration** to a **lower** one.
Blood arriving here has come back from your body's cells, so it's **low in oxygen** and **high in carbon dioxide**.
The fresh air in the alveolus is the opposite: **high in oxygen**, and low in carbon dioxide.
So **oxygen diffuses** from the air into the blood.
And **carbon dioxide diffuses** from the blood into the air, ready to be breathed out.
**Red blood cells** pick up the oxygen, using a substance called **haemoglobin**, and carry it around your body.
No pumping is needed. It's **passive diffusion**, driven by the difference in concentration: the **concentration gradient**.
Breathing keeps bringing in fresh air, which keeps the gradient **steep**, so diffusion keeps going.
High on a mountain, each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules, so climbers breathe faster, and many carry oxygen tanks.

chapters.title: Alveoli: built for fast gas exchange

lines.cap: Alveoli are a brilliant example of a structure built for its job: every feature makes diffusion **faster**.
Diffusion is faster with a **large surface area**, a **short distance** to travel, and a **steep concentration gradient**.
First, a **huge surface area**. Your alveoli add up to about **70 square metres**, roughly the size of a badminton court, squeezed inside your chest.
Second, **very thin walls**. Each alveolus wall is just **one cell thick**, and so is the capillary wall beside it.
That makes a tiny **diffusion distance**, so the gases cross almost instantly.
Third, a **moist lining**. Gases must **dissolve** before they can diffuse across.
Fourth, a **rich blood supply**. Blood is constantly carried away and replaced, keeping the concentration gradient **steep**.
And **ventilation**, breathing, keeps bringing in fresh air, which keeps the gradient steep too.
Remember **TIMS**: **T**hin walls, lots of blood **I**n the capillaries, a **M**oist lining, and a big **S**urface area.
Together, they let your blood load up with oxygen in a **fraction of a second**, as it flows past.

chapters.title: Inhaled vs exhaled air, and limewater

lines.cap: Breathing changes the air. Comparing the air you breathe in with the air you breathe out is a classic exam table.
**Oxygen**: about **21%** of the air you breathe in, and about **16%** of the air you breathe out.
So breathed-out air still holds plenty of oxygen. That's why **rescue breaths** in CPR can keep someone's cells supplied until help arrives.
**Carbon dioxide**: about **0.04%** in, but about **4%** out. That's around **100 times** more.
**Nitrogen** is the biggest part of air, about **78%**. It's **unchanged**, because your body doesn't use it.
**Water vapour** goes from low to **high**. That's why your breath fogs up a cold window.
And breathed-out air is **warmer**, because your body has warmed it.
To test for carbon dioxide, use **limewater**. It's **clear** to start with, and turns **cloudy**, or milky, when carbon dioxide bubbles through.
Breathe out through one tube of limewater, and draw room air through another. The breathed-out air turns its limewater cloudy much **faster**.
That proves breathed-out air contains far **more carbon dioxide**.
When you exercise, your muscles work harder, so they **respire faster** to release more energy.
So they need **more oxygen**, and they make **more carbon dioxide**, which must be removed.
Your **breathing rate** increases: you take more breaths per minute.
And your **breathing depth** increases: each breath is bigger, moving more air in and out.
What triggers it? Your brain keeps track of the **carbon dioxide** level in your blood.
When it detects **rising carbon dioxide**, it sends signals that make you breathe faster and deeper.
So breathing speeds up because **carbon dioxide is rising**, not simply because your body 'wants more oxygen'.
It's also why you can't hold your breath for long: as carbon dioxide builds up, the urge to breathe becomes overwhelming.
Your **heart rate** rises too, pumping oxygen-rich blood around your body faster.
After you stop, you keep breathing hard for a while, to repay the **oxygen debt**: extra oxygen to break down the **lactic acid** from anaerobic respiration.
Investigate it: count your breaths per minute at rest, then straight after a minute of star jumps, and keep counting as it settles.
A fitter person's breathing gets back to normal faster: a better **recovery rate**.

chapters.title: Smoking and other harm to the lungs

lines.cap: Your gas-exchange system is delicate, and **smoking** is one of the worst things for it.
Tobacco smoke contains **tar**, a sticky brown substance that coats the airways.
Tar contains chemicals that cause **cancer**: it's a **carcinogen**.
Tar also paralyses and destroys the **cilia**. The mucus escalator stops, causing **smoker's cough** and more chest infections.
**Carbon monoxide** is a poisonous gas. It binds to **haemoglobin** more strongly than oxygen does, so the blood carries **less oxygen**.
That strains the heart, and in pregnancy it cuts the oxygen reaching the baby.
**Nicotine** is the **addictive** drug that makes smoking so hard to give up. It also raises heart rate and blood pressure.
Remember: **C**igarettes **C**ause **T**rouble. **C**arbon monoxide, **c**ancer-causing tar, and **t**obacco's nicotine.
Years of smoking can cause **emphysema**: the walls between alveoli break down, merging them into fewer, bigger sacs.
That **reduces the surface area** for gas exchange, so the person is breathless, even at rest.
Smoking also causes **lung cancer** and **bronchitis**.
Other things harm the lungs too. **Asbestos** and fine **dust** scar them, and **air pollution** inflames the airways and makes **asthma** worse.
Science today: **vaping** avoids the tar, so it's seen as less harmful than smoking. But it still delivers addictive nicotine, and its long-term effects aren't known yet.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Tall Brontosaurs Breathe Air**: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
Breathing **IN**: the diaphragm d**i**ps, the ribs r**i**se, the volume r**i**ses, the pressure d**i**ps.
**TIMS**: thin walls, lots of blood in the capillaries, a moist lining and a big surface area.
**Cigarettes Cause Trouble**: carbon monoxide, cancer-causing tar and nicotine.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: breathing is **not** respiration. Breathing moves air; respiration is a chemical reaction in cells.
Two: when you breathe **in**, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles **contract**. They relax when you breathe out.
Three: air rushes in because the **pressure** in your chest falls, not because your lungs pull it in.
Four: oxygen enters the blood by **diffusion**. It isn't pumped.
Five: breathed-out air is still about **16% oxygen**, and only about **4% carbon dioxide**.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
What's the order of the airway, from the trachea down to the air sacs?
**Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.**
When you breathe in, does your diaphragm contract or relax?
It **contracts**, and flattens.
How does oxygen get from the alveoli into your blood?
By **diffusion**, from a high to a low concentration.
What happens to limewater when you breathe out through it?
It turns from clear to **cloudy**, because of the carbon dioxide.
Which gas in cigarette smoke cuts the oxygen your blood can carry?
**Carbon monoxide.**
Brilliant work. Now try the Breathing quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
